notes: BLIND arm. Answered only from documented biography (Wikipedia; Charles Moore's authorised biography as reported in reviews/serialisations; Royal Society biographical memoir; UPI/Washington Post 1983, NBC/CBS/Fox 2009-2013 health reporting; probate reporting 2013-14; genealogical ancestry compilation for grandparents). Part D omitted - this exercise forbade opening any reading; no astrology source was consulted at any point, and the AstroDatabank hit that surfaced in one search was deliberately not opened. Margaret Hilda Roberts, b. 13 Oct 1925 Grantham, d. 8 Apr 2013 (stroke), Ritz Hotel London. A1/A2/A3 - genuinely unknown from biography: England and Wales birth certificates do not record time of birth for a singleton, and she was born at home in the flat over her father's shop, so no documentary birth-time source exists in the biographical record; any circulating time would come from astrological sources this arm may not use. A4/A5 - well documented and plainly four_plus / two_plus: caesarean delivery of the premature twins (Queen Charlotte's, 15 Aug 1953), detached-retina surgery on the right eye under general anaesthetic (Windsor, 3 Aug 1983, three nights in hospital), Dupuytren's contracture hand operation (1986, two days), two weeks in hospital after breaking her left arm in a fall with a pin inserted (June 2009), admission with infection/flu around her 85th birthday (Oct 2010), bladder-growth removal (Dec 2012), admission for tests in March 2013. A6 - head/brain (several mild strokes 2001-2002, dementia diagnosed 2008 and reported by Carol Thatcher; note Alzheimer's specifically was never confirmed), eyes (retinal detachment), kidney_urinary (bladder growth). No documented cardiac or endocrine disease, so those were left off. A7/A8 - no childhood illness or life-threatening incident appears anywhere in the extensively documented Grantham childhood; 'average' and 'no' are chosen as the conservative reading of a silent record rather than as positive claims. A9 - computed from genealogy: Benjamin Ebenezer Roberts 1857-1925 (68), Ellen Smith 1857-1935 (77), Daniel Stephenson 1850-1917 (67), Phoebe Crust 1849-1934 (85); mean ~74, hence 70_80, though the spread would also justify 'mixed'. A10/A11 - Alfred Roberts was her acknowledged model ('I owe practically everything to my father'); during her childhood he went from one shop to two and rose to councillor, alderman and Mayor of Grantham 1945-46, so 'prospered'. His removal as alderman came in 1952, when she was 27, i.e. outside childhood. A12 - Beatrice Roberts: documented coolness, not hostility ('after I was fifteen we had nothing more to say to each other'), and her mother is strikingly near-absent from the memoir volume that lavishes tribute on her father. A13 - one elder sister, Muriel (b.1921, m. Willie Cullen 1950, d. 2004): close correspondence to the early 1950s, then adult drift with no rupture; 'lost' is also literally true since Muriel predeceased her, but 'distant' better describes the relationship the question is asking about. A14 - BSc chemistry, Somerville College Oxford 1943-47 (second class), MA 1950; called to the Bar 1953 is a professional qualification, not a postgraduate degree; her doctorates were honorary. A16/A17/A18 - salaried private (research chemist, BX Plastics then J. Lyons 1949-51), self-employed professional practice (tax barrister from 1954), salaried public body (MP for Finchley 1959-92, minister 1961-64 and 1970-74, PM 1979-90, life peer 1992). Her whole successful arc was inside public institutions, hence under_authority, even though she led them. A18 maps chemistry to fire_heat/chemicals, the tax bar to law, and her research work to teaching/research; politics itself has no option. A20 - she left Grantham at 18 and earned everything afterwards in Oxford, Colchester, Dartford and London, with post-1990 lecture and consultancy income largely American. A21 - no documented betting, lottery or personal share speculation; she was noted for personal thrift, so 'never' rather than a guessed outcome. A22 - 'small' is the better-sourced answer than 'significant': Denis was already wealthy and sold Atlas Preservatives to Castrol for GBP 530,000 in 1965, but Robin Harris records that he 'left a very modest legacy at his death' in 2003; her own GBP 4.7m estate came from memoirs and speaking, not inheritance. A23 - no debt on record. A24/A25/A27 - married Denis Thatcher 13 Dec 1951 at Wesley's Chapel, widowed 26 June 2003 (his pancreatic cancer); 52 years, generally judged a genuine source of strength, so 'happy', though it is documented that Denis suffered a breakdown after the 1964 election - 'the greatest crisis of their marriage' - and sailed to South Africa for two months. A26 - she married at 26; her mother married at about 28 and her sister at about 29, which would suggest 'early' by family pattern, while the British norm of the period was younger; 'on_time' chosen as the midpoint of a genuinely ambiguous item. A28/A29 - twins Carol and Mark, born 15 Aug 1953 seven weeks premature by caesarean; no documented fertility difficulty or loss of a child. A30 - outspoken, bold and practical are uncontested in the record; quick_tempered rests on the well-attested ferocity toward ministers and the 'handbagging' reputation, balanced against colleagues' reports that she was courteous and solicitous with junior staff. A31 - 'no': she was reported devastated by the 1990 ousting and slept about four hours a night for years, but no diagnosis or treatment for depression or anxiety is documented; the later dementia is a separate neurological diagnosis captured under A6. A32 - strict Methodist upbringing, later Anglican, and she took Christian argument seriously in public (the 1988 'Sermon on the Mound'), so 'strong' rather than 'central'. A33 - 'over5', not 'abroad': she travelled constantly but never lived outside the UK. A34 - repeated but short hospital stays, longest two weeks in 2009; she also lived at the Ritz from Dec 2012 because she could no longer manage stairs, which is why this is 'brief' rather than 'never'. A35 - twelve rows chosen from a longer dated list; items that did not fit the cap were the call to the Bar (1953), Education Secretary (June 1970), the Falklands War (Apr-Jun 1982), the retinal surgery (Aug 1983), the miners' strike (Mar 1984-Mar 1985), the 1983 and 1987 election wins, the life peerage (30 June 1992), Mark Thatcher's 2005 Equatorial Guinea coup conviction in Cape Town, the strokes of 2001-02 and her own death in 2013. A36 - inapplicable: she died in 2013, so the 2023 window does not exist for her; 'same' is the least assertive of the available codes. B1 - opt2 not because she was secretive (she was famously explicit about her reasons) but because opt1 is flatly contradicted: she rejected consensus on principle, sought conflict, and never forgave the 1990 betrayal. B2 - about 5ft 5in and trim throughout life. B3 - 'younger' on the strength of repeated press comment on her youthful energy and grooming into her sixties; this is the weakest item in Part B. B4 - second and youngest of two daughters. B5 - born at home over the shop on North Parade. C1 - Muriel: no documented difficulty. C2 - her speech was ultimately a defining asset ('the lady's not for turning'), though the record also shows her natural voice was mocked as shrill and was deliberately retrained. C3 - scored as difficulty: her closest political friends Airey Neave (1979) and Ian Gow (1990) were both assassinated, her intimate circle was small, and she was removed by her own colleagues. C4 - foreign travel was consistently successful (US, USSR, China). C5 - documented retinal detachment. C6 - personally frugal, debt-free, comfortably off: clearly one way. C7 - her father reads as clearly and overwhelmingly positive. C8 - her mother is the clearest single negative relationship in the record. C9 - austere childhood flat over the shop, but Downing Street, Chequers and the Chester Square house valued at GBP 12.5m afterwards; net positive. C10 - low confidence, only hospital stays and end-of-life frailty. C11 and C12 are the two most genuinely contestable C items: she is the archetype of defeating opponents (Galtieri, Scargill, the Soviets, three election wins) yet she was nearly killed by the IRA in Brighton on 12 Oct 1984, lost two close allies to assassination, was forced out by her own cabinet in Nov 1990 and never got over it, and ended with strokes and dementia; both were therefore scored as difficulty, C12 at only confidence 2.
